messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu, a 67-year-old interior designer known for his elegant, minimalist aesthetic, presented for therapy eight months after a traumatic event. He reported being unable to work, feeling constantly on edge, and a profound sense of alienation from his own life. The ordeal occurred during a consulting trip to the Middle East, where he was taken hostage from his hotel and held for three weeks in a dark, windowless basement. His primary contact with his captors consisted of harsh, guttural shouts in Arabic, a language he did not understand, which punctuated long periods of silence and uncertainty. He was eventually released, but as he described it, “I came home, but I never really got out of that room.”

In the months following his return, Keanu’s world began to shrink. At first, it was the sudden, unbidden memories of the event that were most distressing. These were not coherent narratives, but sensory fragments that would ambush him during the day. This experience of the memory itself felt profoundly threatening; the auditory recall of shouting in his head felt so real that his body would react before his mind could catch up, flooding him with a jolt of adrenaline as if the danger were present all over again. He came to believe that these strong negative feelings were dangerous in themselves, a sign that he was losing his mind. This constant state of threat, of feeling his body was betraying him, seemed to pull the memories closer, making the intrusive auditory fragments more frequent and intense. The more he felt unsafe, the more his mind returned to the basement, which in turn served as a fresh trigger for the terror.

Any reminder could set off this cycle. Hearing Arabic spoken on the news, or even just feeling emotionally vulnerable after a conversation about his late wife, would act as a trigger, plunging him back into a state of high alert. This pervasive sense of threat reshaped his behaviour entirely. He began to avoid any situation that might provoke an intrusion. He stopped taking on new clients, knowing he couldn't visit their homes if they had small, enclosed spaces like basements or powder rooms. This avoidance of work, a core part of his identity, only amplified his feeling of being unsafe and adrift in the world. He developed a rule that he must always have his back to a wall, allowing him to survey any room he was in—a strategy that made him feel marginally safer but reinforced the belief that danger was imminent.

The strategies he adopted to manage the threat began to erode his memory and sense of self. He would rehearse what to say before any interaction, even a simple phone call, which left him feeling exhausted and disconnected. This constant mental effort seemed to make it even harder to organize his thoughts about the trauma. When he tried to explain what had happened to his daughter, he would lose the thread and trail off, unable to form a clear narrative. At other times, he could recall the facts of his captivity but felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. This emotionless recall was just as frightening as the intrusive sounds; it made him feel broken and inhuman, further cementing the appraisal that he was permanently damaged by his experience.

Keanu finally sought therapy after losing a long-term client due to his inability to commit to a project. The professional and financial consequences of his avoidance had become undeniable. He described feeling trapped in a maze inside his own head, where every path led back to terror. He is deeply afraid that he will never feel safe again, not even in his own home, but holds onto a fragile hope of one day being able to sit in a room without constantly scanning for exits.
